opening_summary: Twenty ideas for aiming a game camera, from turning and moving it to changing its lens, telling a dolly from a zoom, and following the player. With the exact word, an AI coding agent builds the shot you want.
opening_description: 20 camera terms: turn, move, lens, follow.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers say zoom in when they mean move the camera closer. Those are two different things. A zoom changes the lens, and the camera stays where it is. A dolly moves the camera, so near and far things shift against each other. This film goes through twenty camera terms in five groups, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
A zoom means
moving the camera closer.
idea.replacementWords: changing the lens, not the place

beats.narration: This table is the map. Twenty camera ideas, in five groups, and each one says what changed. The first group turns the camera on the spot, with pan, tilt and roll. The direction changes, and the position stays.

The second group moves the camera. Dolly, in and out, truck, pedestal and orbit. Here the position changes. A dolly, truck or pedestal keeps facing the same way, and an orbit turns to keep its subject in view.
The third group changes the lens. Zoom, focal length, field of view, and perspective versus orthographic. What changes is the angle the camera takes in, and how big things look.
The fourth group tells look-alikes apart, with dolly versus zoom, and parallax. The question here is whether near things and far things shift against each other.

The fifth group follows the action. Follow camera, smoothing, also called damping, deadzone, look-ahead, screen shake and camera limits. These say how a camera trails a player, waits, leads, jolts and stops.

Three small drawings of a camera that turns but never moves. The first is seen from above. Pan means turning left or right on the spot. Here the camera turns twenty-five degrees, its position unchanged, and the red post comes into view. A pan turns, while a truck moves sideways. For example, in a cutscene the camera stands by the gate and pans right, from the player to a door that has just opened.

The middle drawing is seen from the side. Tilt means turning up or down on the spot. The camera pitches up twenty-five degrees, its position unchanged, and the two upper posts turn red as they come into view. For example, at the start of a level the camera stands at the foot of a tower and tilts up to show the goal flag at the top.

The last drawing shows what the camera sees. Roll means spinning the camera around the direction it looks along, so the horizon tips. Here it rolls twenty-five degrees, and the flat ground now runs downhill across the picture. Pan and tilt change where the camera points, and roll does not. For example, when the player's plane banks into a turn, the view rolls with it and the horizon slopes across the screen.

A top view and a side view of a camera that moves but keeps facing the same way. Dolly means moving the camera forward or backward along the way it looks. Dolly in moves toward the subject, and dolly out moves away. Here the camera dollies in one point five metres, then back out. For example, before a boss fight the camera dollies in toward the boss, so it grows in the frame as the camera travels.

Truck means moving the camera left or right while it keeps facing the same way. In the top view it trucks right and then left, one point one metres, and the view cone never turns. A pan would turn the cone instead. For example, in a side-on cutscene the camera trucks right alongside a character running past a row of shops, looking straight at them the whole time.

Pedestal means moving the camera straight up or down while it keeps facing the same way. In the side view it rises and falls zero point nine metres, still looking straight ahead. Tilt turns the camera upward, and pedestal lifts the whole camera. For example, as the player rides an elevator up a shaft, the camera pedestals up with it, looking straight ahead the whole way.

A top view of a subject in the middle of a circle. Orbit means moving around a subject on a curved path while keeping it framed. The camera sweeps one hundred forty degrees around the circle, always one point nine metres away and always aimed at the subject, so the subject never leaves the frame. For example, on a character select screen the camera orbits the chosen hero, so the player sees them from every side.

Now a sweep done as a pan instead. The camera stays where it is and turns seventy degrees. Half its view is only twenty degrees wide, so the subject passes out of the frame. An orbit keeps the subject, and a pan can lose it. For example, if you ask an agent to circle the hero and it writes a pan, the hero drifts off the edge of the select screen.

A top view of a camera fixed at the left. Zoom means changing the lens, its field of view or focal length, while the camera stays put. Here a one hundred thirty-five millimetre lens narrows the cone to fifteen point two degrees, and things look three point eight six times bigger than with a thirty-five millimetre lens. A dolly would move the camera instead. For example, aiming down a scope in a first-person game zooms the view while the player stands still.

Focal length is the strength of the lens, in millimetres. A longer focal length gives a narrower view and more magnification. In the table, with the sensor width the drawing assumes, twenty-four millimetres takes in seventy-three point seven degrees, and two hundred millimetres only ten point three, at five point seven one times. For example, to make a far-off castle fill the frame in a cutscene, give the camera a longer focal length rather than moving it.

Field of view, or FOV, is the same lens described as an angle. A wider field of view shows more. At ninety degrees, seven of the nine posts are in view, and on the sensor assumed here that is an eighteen millimetre lens. For example, a first-person game can offer a field of view setting in its options menu, and a wider setting shows more of the room at the edges of the screen.

Two pictures of one scene, a dark house near the camera and a red tower far behind it. Dolly versus zoom comes down to parallax, near and far shifting against each other. In the dolly the camera moves one point two metres forward. The near house grows one point six seven times, and the far tower only one point one five. For example, a cutscene that dollies toward the hero makes the hero grow while the mountains behind barely change.

Now the zoom. The camera stays put and the lens magnifies one point six seven times. The house grows just as much as it did in the dolly, but now the tower grows one point six seven times too. A zoom only magnifies. For example, zoom toward the same hero and the mountains behind swell along with them, and nothing shifts against anything else.

Same house, different tower. Compare the house's width to the tower's. In the dolly that ratio goes from two point seven to three point nine. In the zoom it stays at two point seven. That ratio is how you tell the two apart in a finished shot. For example, if the player grows much faster than the background, the camera moved, and if both grow together, it zoomed.

A top view of a camera beside three posts in a line, and the picture it sees. Parallax means nearer things shift more than farther things when the viewpoint moves. The camera trucks one metre to the right. The posts were lined up, and now they fan out in the picture. A zoom would scale everything by the same factor. For example, as a side-scrolling platformer follows the player, the near bushes rush past while the far hills creep.

The bars give the shift for each post. The near post, two metres away, moves one hundred ten pixels. The middle post at four metres moves fifty-five, and the far post at eight metres moves twenty-eight. Half the distance, twice the shift. For example, a platformer with two background layers should move its far layer less than its near layer as the camera follows the player.

Two rows of boxes that are all the same size in the world. Perspective means distant things shrink. Here the nearest box, three metres away, is eighty-seven pixels wide, and the farthest, at thirteen metres, is twenty. The rows draw together toward the horizon. For example, a third-person game uses a perspective camera, so an enemy far down a corridor looks small and grows as it comes nearer.

Now the same boxes seen by an orthographic camera. Orthographic means size does not depend on distance. Every box is forty-four pixels wide wherever it stands, and the rows stay parallel and never meet. Perspective shrinks the far boxes, and orthographic does not. For example, a puzzle game seen from above at an angle can use an orthographic camera, so a crate at the back of the room is drawn the same size as one at the front.

A view window over a moving red dot, in this simulated run. A follow camera tracks a moving target, usually with smoothing. In the top lane the window is locked to the target. The camera's position equals the target's on every frame, so the lag is zero pixels. For example, in a platformer the camera follows the player across the level, so the player stays on screen while they run.

Smoothing, also called damping, spreads the camera's catch-up over time, so it trails the target slightly instead of snapping to it. In the lower lane the window falls behind as the dot speeds up, by as much as one hundred three pixels, then eases in and settles at zero. The time constant is zero point two five seconds. For example, when the player dashes, a smoothed camera lags a moment and glides after them instead of jerking.

A screen frame with a dashed box in the middle, in this simulated run. A deadzone is a region of the screen where the target can move without the camera moving. The red dot walks right inside the box, and the view stays still. At the edge of the box, seventy pixels from the centre, the camera follows. In all it moved two hundred seventy pixels. For example, a platformer hero can shuffle back and forth without the screen jiggling.

Look-ahead shifts the framing toward the direction of travel. The target moves right at two hundred pixels per second, and the frame looks half a second ahead, to where the target will be, so it shifts one hundred pixels forward. The dot sits behind the centre cross, with room in front. A deadzone waits, and look-ahead leans. For example, in a runner game the camera shows more ground ahead of the running player, so they see the next gap in time to jump.

A small view of a scene, in this simulated run. Screen shake is a brief, fading, random offset of the camera, for impact. A hit lands, and the view jumps by up to eighteen pixels in a random direction, less on every frame, until the most it can jump is zero point six pixels. Shake adds jerk on purpose, and smoothing takes it away. For example, when an enemy's attack hits the player, the screen jolts for a moment, so the hit is felt.

The graph traces the sideways offset over zero point six seconds. The black line jumps from side to side but stays inside the red dashed curve, which keeps falling. It drops to five percent, zero point nine pixels, after zero point five four seconds, and the shot is steady again. For example, an explosion behind the player can shake the view hard at first and then let it settle fast, so play goes on.

A long strip of level, with a hatched empty area past its right edge, in this simulated run. Camera limits are clamps that keep the view inside the level. Without them the view follows the target to five hundred ninety, and its right edge ends up seventy pixels past the end of the level. The player sees the void. For example, when the hero reaches the last wall of a level, a camera without limits shows empty space beyond it.

Now with camera limits. The view's centre is clamped between one hundred twenty and five hundred twenty, so its edges never leave the level. The target still walks on to five hundred ninety, and the view stops at the edge. A deadzone is a box on the screen, and limits are the edges of the level. For example, give the platformer camera limits so it stops at the left wall of the first room.

Each pair puts two look-alike moves side by side. Pan turns the camera on the spot, here forty degrees, and it stays in the same place. Truck moves the camera sideways, here zero point seven metres, still facing the same way.

Dolly moves the camera forward, here one point two metres, and its view angle stays at forty-six degrees. Zoom keeps the camera put and narrows the angle to twenty-two degrees. Both make the subject bigger, in different ways.
Orbit moves the camera around the subject on a curve, and the subject stays framed. Pan turns the camera on the spot, and here the subject is lost from view.

Smoothing, or damping, starts moving at once and eases toward the target, trailing slightly. The red line is the target and the black line the camera. A deadzone camera waits, then follows, and stops short of the target.

Vague requests on the left, each with the exact instruction that replaces it. Swoop in becomes, dolly in two metres, one point five seconds, ease-out. The graph shows it start at four metres per second and slow to zero as it arrives.
Look around a bit becomes, pan right forty degrees, two seconds, ease-in-out. That means slow, fast, slow, with a top speed of fifty-nine degrees per second.

Get closer could mean a dolly or a zoom, and the exact version picks one. Zoom from thirty-five millimetres to eighty-five, in one second, ease-in-out, and the camera stays put. The angle narrows from fifty-four point four degrees to twenty-three point nine.
Make the hit feel heavier becomes, screen shake, zero point three seconds, twelve pixels, fading to zero. The curve shows the shake shrinking, with five percent left at zero point three seconds.

Follow the player nicely becomes, follow with smoothing, a zero point two five second time constant, and a deadzone one hundred forty by one hundred pixels. The camera closes ninety-five percent of the gap after zero point seven five seconds, three time constants.
This is a checklist to run before you give a camera instruction. First, is the camera moving, with a dolly, truck, pedestal or orbit, or turning, with a pan, tilt or roll?
Second, is it the legs or the lens? A dolly moves the camera, and a zoom changes the lens. Only the dolly makes near and far things shift against each other.
Third, did you name the axis, the direction, how far or how many degrees, how long, and the easing? An AI coding agent cannot guess any of them.
Fourth, for a camera that follows a player, give the smoothing amount, the deadzone size, the look-ahead, and the camera limits.
Fifth, for a hit, give the shake size and how long it lasts, and say that it fades to zero.

Sixth, for the lens and projection, give the focal length or the field of view, and say perspective or orthographic. Then say it exactly. Dolly in two metres, one point five seconds, ease-out, not swoop in.

recap_lines: Pan, tilt and roll turn the camera on the spot.
Dolly, truck and pedestal move the camera and keep it facing the same way.
An orbit circles the subject and keeps it framed, where a pan can lose it.
A zoom changes the lens, and a dolly moves the camera.
Parallax means near things shift more than far ones when the camera moves.
A deadzone waits, smoothing trails, look-ahead leads, and limits stop the view.

your_turn.segment: Name The Camera Move, Defend It
your_turn.command: Quiz me on camera terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use pan, tilt, truck, pedestal, dolly, zoom, orbit, parallax, deadzone and look-ahead. Describe what a camera does in a game or a cutscene, and I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case describes a camera in a game, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 1, row 'Move the camera': the WHAT CHANGES cell says 'The position; the view direction stays', but orbit is in the same row and an orbit turns the camera to keep the subject framed (slide 5 shows the view direction sweeping 140°). True for dolly, truck and pedestal only. The narration says so.
Slide 7 step 3: 'that is a 18 mm lens on the 36 mm sensor' should read 'an 18 mm lens'.

Slide 10 step 1: in the perspective drawing the boxes overlap into two solid staircase shapes just under the horizon (renderProj: the 3 m box spans about x 216 to 302 and the 4.5 m box about 270 to 328), so the five separate boxes and the converging rows are hard to see, and the dashed row lines are hidden under the boxes.

Slide 5: the notes say the pan is 'the same angle' and the step 2 caption says 'The same sweep done as a pan', but the orbit sweeps 140° and the pan turns 70°. The narration says only 'a sweep done as a pan'.

Slide 15 step 2: 'limits: x between 120 and 520 px, so half the 200 px view stays inside' reads as if only half the view stays in the level. It means the view's half-width (100 px) is kept inside each level edge (20 and 620).
Slide 4 step 1 and slide 12 step 1 show their TELL THESE APART box (Pedestal vs Tilt; Smoothing vs Deadzone) before the first term in it has been defined on that slide.
